articles.title_orig: Israel Election Live Updates: Record Voter Turnout as Netanyahu Faces Challenge Led by Eisenkot
articles.title_zh: Israel Election Live Updates: Record Voter Turnout as Netanyahu Faces Challenge Led by Eisenkot
articles.content_orig:
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu casts his ballot, alongside his wife Sara, at a polling station in Jerusalem on Oct. 27, 2026.
Israelis headed to polling stations in record numbers on Tuesday to decide the political fate of Benjamin Netanyahu , the country’s longest-serving Prime Minister who is facing one of the most consequential tests of his decadeslong political career.
Netanyahu was joined by his wife Sara as he cast his ballot just after midday, local time, at a polling station in a Jerusalem school. “This is a very moving and fateful moment. My wife and I are truly overwhelmed,” Netanyahu told reporters after voting. “We know what is at stake, and since I am not allowed to say things explicitly, I will say: Vote correctly.”
From 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. local time (1 a.m. to 4 p.m. EDT), Israelis can cast votes for representatives in the Knesset. Numbers from Israel's Central Elections ​Committee reflect a strong turnout, with 66.7% of eligible voters reported to have cast their ballots by 6 p.m., local time. It is understood to be the highest turnout logged at this time since since 1973.
Hours after the polls opened, Netanyahu told his supporters that "buses are heading to the polling stations and huge lines are being reported in the Arab settlements." Complaining that "the right-wing strongholds are not waking up," he again urged people to go out and vote.
Netanyahu’s Likud party said in a statement that it had submitted a request to the Central Elections Committee to extend voting hours past 10 p.m. The committee later said it would not be extend voting hours past the scheduled closing time.
This is the first election in the country since the Oct. 7, 2023 terrorist attacks by Palestinian militant group Hamas and the subsequent Israeli war in the Gaza Strip . Since then, Israel under Netanyahu has pursued an aggressive military campaign across the Middle East—going to war with Iran , backing settler attacks and displacement in the West Bank, and carrying out strikes against militant groups in Lebanon and Yemen .
Tuesday’s election is widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership and Israelis’ willingness to change course amid uncertainty. According to polls, the outcome is far from certain, with a tight race expected as Israel decides upon its future.
Read More: Israel's Choice
“I hope this will be a true holiday for democracy,” Isaac Herzog, the Israeli head of state, told reporters from a polling station in Rehavia, where he and his wife voted. “No one can be allowed to spoil or undermine it.”
Two main political blocs are contending to form Israel’s next government. The first is the pro-Netanyahu coalition led by Netanyahu’s Likud party. The coalition includes far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties, such as Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) led by national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Religious Zionism-Zehut led by finance minister Bezalel Smotrich. Their ultranationalist policies have found an audience in younger right-wing Israelis.
On the other side are the Jewish-led opposition movements—with former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot and the centrist Yashar (Straight) party at the forefront. Eisenkot, who entered politics in 2022, joined Netanyahu’s emergency war cabinet after the Oct. 7 attack on Israel. But after having lost a son in combat in Israel’s wars, Eisenkot left his post in 2024. Two of his nephews also died fighting in Gaza, a prominent campaign talking point.
The opposition also includes a joint ticket led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and Knesset opposition leader Yair Lapid, the secular nationalist party Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home) led by former finance minister Avigdor Lieberman, and the Democrats led by former IDF deputy chief of staff Yair Golan.
The Democrats party on Tuesday said Golan had been “approached in a threatening manner” by a man who was found to be carrying a knife. The lawmaker was attending a voting-day mobilization tour in Tel Aviv's HaMesila Park at the time of the incident.
"Golan’s security guards blocked the man, and as they moved toward him, a large knife slipped from beneath his clothing and fell to the ground," the party said in a statement shared with the Guardian . "Police were called to the scene and arrested the suspect." Golan, in his own statement, vowed that "incitement and violence will not deter us" and encouraged people to go out and vote.
Meanwhile, some polls suggest that Eisenkot’s Yashar party may garner slightly more support than Netanyahu’s Likud, but they also project that neither the Prime Minister’s right-wing bloc nor the opposition may win the 61 Knesset seats needed to form a government.
Including Arab parties such as United Arab List (Ra’am) and the Joint List, or fringe parties, could be necessary to form a government. Both pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu coalitions have so far ruled out teaming up with the Arab-led parties. Arab citizens of Israel make up about 20% of the population, though they receive fewer government services and endure higher poverty and unemployment rates . Discrimination and disappointment have historically depressed Arab-Israeli voter turnout.
A cyclist rides beneath a pedestrian bridge displaying electronic election billboards showing former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot (L) and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (R) in Tel Aviv, Israel, on Oct. 23, 2026. Erik Marmor—picture alliance/Getty Images
Netanyahu hopes to maintain his premiership with the help of his longstanding ally, U.S. President Donald Trump , who only announced his endorsement days before the election as conflict in the Middle East has tested their friendship.
In a late-night TV appearance on Oct. 25 , Netanyahu boasted of Trump’s endorsement and said that Trump was willing to take action “that would finally, finally, remove the Iranian threat” so long as Netanyahu stayed in power. Netanyahu added that he has already instructed Israel’s national intelligence agency Mossad as well as the IDF to “bring down” the Iranian regime. Trump remains very popular in Israel.
By contrast, U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance declined to endorse Netanyahu for re-election, just a day after Trump put his “complete and total” support behind the Israeli leader.
“The President has the most effective endorsement in American, or international, political history,” said Vance, when asked in an interview if he would also be extending an endorsement of his own. “I endorse American candidates and that’s where I'm focused on, is the midterms, so I'm not getting involved in the Israeli elections.”
When pushed for an answer, Vance added: “I'm not anti-endorsing [Netanyahu], I'm not pro-endorsing him.”
At stake for Netanyahu could be more than his continued leadership. The premier faces an international arrest warrant for alleged crimes related to the Israeli military campaign in Gaza. And even domestically, critics have demanded an inquiry into Netanyahu’s decision-making around Oct. 7. The attack, which resulted in over 1,200 people in Israel killed and around 250 hostages taken, is considered by many to be indicative of a major security failure.
The Gaza health ministry reports that since Oct. 7, 2023, more than 74,000 individuals have been killed. In the absence of independent monitoring on the ground, Gaza’s health ministry is the primary source for casualty data relied upon by humanitarian groups, journalists, and international bodies. Its figures do not differentiate between civilians and combatants and cannot be independently verified by TIME.
Another issue driving the election is public fury over ultra-Orthodox communities’ exemption from military conscription for men engaged in religious studies. Despite a shortage of soldiers, less than 10% of eligible ultra-Orthodox men enlist, amid demands from Netanyahu’s allies to exempt them. Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main rival, has promised to end the de facto exemptions.

articles.title_orig: From 'Mobut' to Mao, Mbappe dictator meme turns self-mockery into China storm
articles.title_zh: From 'Mobut' to Mao, Mbappe dictator meme turns self-mockery into China storm
articles.content_orig:
By WILL HALLOWELL, NEWS REPORTER
Published: 04:53 EDT, 27 October 2026 | Updated: 11:40 EDT, 27 October 2026
Kylian Mbappe has been dropped by Chinese brands while state TV stations have suspended all LaLiga broadcasts following a joke about Mao Zedong.
A video circulated online in which the French Real Madrid superstar apparently mocked the former Chinese Communist Party leader.
In the footage, he said the funniest internet meme he had seen was of his face photo-shopped onto that of 'some guy – I think he's a Chinese dictator'.
Mbappe has apologised for the 'ill-judged' joke, saying he has 'deep respect' for China and its history.
Meanwhile LaLiga president Javier Medrano has also been forced to weigh in and apologise to China, describing Mbappe's comments as 'offensive' and adding that the Spanish league is 'taking measures... to overcome this situation'.
In China, jokes about Mao – the country's founding leader who died in 1976 – are considered disrespectful and remain a social taboo.
Mbappe had brand deals with the drinks giant Dongpeng and China's largest dairy producer Mengniu, who have now cut ties with the 27-year-old.
Adverts showing AI-generated images of the France captain drinking a Dongpeng sports drink were regularly shown in China during this year's World Cup.
Chinese brands have dropped French football star Kylian Mbappe after he 'joked' about former leader Mao Zedong
In China, jokes about Mao – the country's founding leader who died in 1976 – are considered disrespectful and remain a social taboo
The meme that football fans had created photoshopping Mbappe's face onto Mao, which he references in the video
Those firms have now dropped Mbappe after accusing him of offending the nation.
China Media Group, the state broadcaster, has also reportedly stopped broadcasting LaLiga matches and advertisements involving Mbappe, citing the Frenchman's 'seriously negative conduct' concerning China, according to EFE .
Dongpeng said in a statement: 'Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments.'
The drinks giant added that 'with immediate effect we are terminating all co-operation with Kylian Mbappe'.
Mengniu said in a statement: 'With immediate effect our company is terminating all co-operation with Kylian Mbappe.
'Mengniu firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people.'
Until this incident, Mbappe was hugely popular among Chinese fans with millions of followers on social media.
Mbappe is fondly nicknamed 'Guigui', the Chinese translation of 'Turtle', due to his perceived similarity to one of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles.
A bus featuring Mbappe for Dongpeng's Bushuila electrolyte drink is seen on a street in Shanghai
Mengniu milk products are seen on a shelf at a store in Beijing. The brand has dropped Mbappe after his 'joke' about Mao
Mbappe seen on bottles of one of Dongpeng's electrolyte drinks
The centre-forward's comments in the video were an apparent reference to a meme of Mbappe superimposed on an image of Mao, one of several using the footballer's face and other historical figures.
In a statement on Tuesday, Mbappe said: 'During a recent interview, I reacted to an image of myself.
'My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world.
'I apologise to everyone my words have upset. This was absolutely not my intention.
'I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history. I am sincerely sorry.'
LaLiga president Mr Medrano said: 'From LaLiga, we deeply regret the statements made by Kylian Mbappe that have caused discomfort and offense in China.
'We understand the harm caused and, on behalf of LaLiga I wish to convey our sincere apologies to the Chinese people.
'For many years, we have built a relationship of respect, trust and co-operation with China, its authorities, its sports institutions, its audiovisual operators, and millions of fans of Spanish football.
'We cannot allow an individual action to tarnish that relationship or harm the more than 20 clubs in our professional competitions and millions of Chinese fans.
'We are taking the measures within our reach and working directly with our partners and interlocutors in China to overcome this situation.
'Our commitment to China, its people, and its institutions is steadfast. A relationship built over so many years cannot be damaged by a single episode.'
Four topics related to Mbappe were still among the top ten trending searches on China's social media platform Weibo on Tuesday morning.
Some users called for China to 'blacklist' Mbappe and reduce his commercial value to zero. These comments received hundreds of likes.
Fans have been creating memes superimposing Mbappe's face on images of military and political leaders to suggest that he has the power to call the shots at the teams he plays for.
In an interview with L'Equipe last month, Mbappe said that while some aspects of the meme trend were harmless fun, the viral ones depicting him as a dictator showed 'a lack of political and human awareness'.
When asked about the incident, a spokesman for China's Foreign Ministry said that words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people 'will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society'.
Mbappe has now apologised for the offence caused by his joke, which the France star admitted was 'ill-judged'
'Dongpeng Beverage ends cooperation with Mbappe' has been the top-trending topic on Chinese social media site Weibo.
One Weibo user said that the 'extremely serious wrong remarks... crossed the red line. They are completely unacceptable'.
Others urged Dongpeng to remove Mbappe's image from their energy drink bottles.
Dongqiudi, one of China's biggest online football outlets, said on Monday evening that Mbappe's remarks were 'offensive to China and the Chinese people' and 'have hurt the feelings of Chinese football fans and the Chinese people'.
Mbappe in September addressed a previous meme depicting him as a military dictator, in an interview with French sports newspaper L'Equipe.
He said: 'There's a part of it that's funny. You can tell that, for some people, it's all in good fun.
'But there is another part that's a bit less funny because of the damage such people have caused throughout history.'
The 27-year-old added: 'Being compared to individuals who murder others, or who have brought misery to millions upon millions of people – well, I don't think I've ever done anything like that in my life.'
The furore in China came a day after Mbappe lost out to Harry Kane for the Ballon d'Or, the most prestigious individual award in football.
Global sports stars who have commented on sensitive topics such as Taiwan, Tibet and Hong Kong have previously caused controversy in China and been dumped by sponsors there.
Former NBA player Dwight Howard referred to Taiwan as a country in 2023 as he appeared in a video with the island's vice president and current president Lai Ching-te, sparking fury on Chinese social media.
Beijing claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to bring it under its control.
Houston Rockets general manager Daryl Morey posted a tweet in 2019 supporting Hong Kong protests, leading to China suspending sponsorship deals with the NBA and pulling games off Chinese television for a year.
Chinese media outlets reacted with fury to Mbappe's comments on Tuesday.
'A remark about an internet meme has triggered a backlash among his Chinese fans, threatened his lucrative commercial relationships and offered a sharp reminder of the limits of celebrity influence,' state media outlet China Daily said.
'What did he say? Many Chinese would rather not repeat it,' the state-backed Global Times said.

articles.title_orig: Fed meeting live updates: Federal Reserve weighs elevated inflation, midterm elections as October meeting kicks off
articles.title_zh: Fed meeting live updates: Federal Reserve weighs elevated inflation, midterm elections as October meeting kicks off
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Reserve is scheduled to meet this week, when U.S. central bankers will decide whether to raise interest rates for the second time this year in a bid to subdue inflation.
Most economists and Wall Street analysts expect the Fed to leave its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4% when officials release the latest policy statement on Wednesday.
Consumer prices have surged this year, with headline inflation across the U.S. rising at a 3.7% annual rate in September as energy costs jumped. Core inflation, which excludes volatile energy and gas categories, rose 2.6% from a year ago amid signs inflation could be seeping into the broader economy. The Fed targets annual inflation of 2%.
Gasoline prices, which have hovered above $4 a gallon for the last three months, accounted for more than half the September increase in consumer prices, according to the Labor Department.
"Although the latest hot inflation readings and rise in inflation expectations will concern Fed officials, they still appear broadly intent on tightening policy at a measured pace," Thomas Ryan, senior North America economist at investor advisory firm Capital Economics, said in a recent research note.
In September, the Fed raised the federal funds rate — what banks charge each other for overnight loans — by a quarter of a percentage point — its first hike in three years, thereby raising borrowing costs across the U.S. economy. The Fed is scheduled to announce its latest interest rate decision at 2 p.m. ET on Wednesday.
The meeting comes at a crucial time, as Americans head to the polls to cast their ballots in the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Many Americans have expressed frustration with the state of the economy as they contend with rising costs of gas, food, utilities and other expenses.
Most economists and investors expect the Fed to raise rates one more time before year-end, likely at its last meeting of the year on Dec. 8-9.
According to CME Group's Fed Watch tool, which uses 30-day Fed funds futures prices to predict rate decisions, traders see an 88% probability that the Fed will hold rates steady in October and a 71% probability the Fed will raise rates in December (no meeting scheduled for November).
In quarterly projections last month, the Fed signaled that its rate-setting committee expected to raise rates later this year. At the same time, some Fed policymakers have signaled that the central bank is in no rush to lift borrowing costs.
"With the policy action we took at our September meeting, there is no need for urgency, and we have time to gather more information," New York Fed President John Williams said in a speech at the University at Buffalo following the Fed's rate hike in September.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh will give a press conference after this week's rate decision. Until then, investors are unlikely to get any clues from Warsh, who has argued against sharing forward guidance on rate decisions.

articles.title_orig: Dollar General overcharged millions at checkout for years, FTC and 20 states allege
articles.title_zh: Dollar General overcharged millions at checkout for years, FTC and 20 states allege
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Trade Commission and 20 states on Monday sued Dollar General, accusing the budget retailer of charging customers more for products than it advertised.
The chain, which operates 21,000 stores nationwide, allegedly mislabeled prices for years, "extracting millions of dollars in unlawful overcharges," the FTC alleged.
"Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last," Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement .
The FTC added that American consumers depend on Dollar General's advertised low prices to make ends meet on tight budgets, while prices that don't reflect advertised deals make it impossible for them to manage household finances.
The agency filed its complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee, Dollar General's home state.
"Our goal is 100% accuracy between shelf and register prices in every store," Dollar General said in a statement. "As with other retailers and despite our policies and procedures, occasional price discrepancies can occur. When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered, and expected to make things right for the customer. In recent years, we have enhanced our price-accuracy processes and remain committed to continuous improvement."
Dollar General said it was made aware of the FTC's investigation in early February.
According to the suit, thousands of Dollar General stores unlawfully overcharged shoppers.
Dollar General "has for years engaged in deceptive conduct that harms the very consumers it claims to serve," the FTC and states allege in the suit. "Although Dollar General promises convenience, low prices, and value, the company has routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on shelves, price tags, and advertisements. This pattern of inaccurate pricing has persisted for years and affects millions of purchases across the country."
The company also faced thousands of consumer complaints claiming it failed to honor advertised prices at checkout, a sign Dollar General knowingly harmed customers, according to the FTC.
The suit seeks a permanent injunction, along with monetary and other relief.
In its statement, Dollar General said, "FTC staff also demanded a monetary amount that was untethered to — and orders of magnitude larger than — any realistic assessment of amounts attributable to pricing discrepancies."
The company said it "worked tirelessly and in good faith to resolve this matter without litigation," including an "alternative, and in our view, more reasonable, manner of calculating potential settlement ranges."
"Although we respect the FTC's role in protecting American consumers and the State representatives' role in protecting the citizens of their respective states, we will defend this litigation vigorously," it said.
The FTC leveled the unfair pricing allegations against Dollar General as other retailers face scrutiny over how they charge shoppers. Consumer advocates say retailers are developing new artificial intelligence-enabled technology that could be used to charge consumers different prices .
Groundwork Collaborative, a nonprofit think tank focused on economic policy, led an investigation into grocery-shopping platform Instacart and found that in a trial, it had used AI to simultaneously show customers different prices for the same goods from the same store.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow stays flat, Nasdaq and S&P 500 surge as oil prices fall and chip stocks bounce
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow stays flat, Nasdaq and S&P 500 surge as oil prices fall and chip stocks bounce
articles.content_orig:
The pace at which investors are borrowing money to invest in stocks has cooled substantially, raising concern that the stock market may be due for a fall.
Recent FINRA data shows the annual growth in margin debt fell to 31.4% in September from 53.7% in May, Bank of America technical strategist Paul Ciana pointed out in a Friday note. Ciana warned that slowing borrowing momentum from extreme levels has been associated with previous market peaks.
May's growth rate in 2026 was the fourth highest since 1998, according to a BofA analysis. The three higher extremes took place in 2000, 2007 and 2021 — all of which preceded stock market declines.
Earlier this year, borrowing was increasing much faster than stocks were rising. Analysts view high borrowing levels as a contrarian signal, similar to bull-bear sentiment indicators.
At $1.48 trillion, margin debt in September is 1.5% below June's record of $1.5 trillion.
High leverage can have snowball effects in a market downturn. Lower prices trigger demands for additional collateral or forced sales, which accelerate a downturn.
Individual investors can be hit hard. Tesla investor Hy Luu, for example, refinanced his home to raise $30,000 to pay down margin debt during the stock's 2022 decline.
BofA sees other market warning signs, including widening high-yield credit spreads and a rotation toward defensive sectors like healthcare and consumer staples.
Paradoxically, the rotation into those sectors has pushed them to "bubble-risk levels," BofA's equity derivatives team said in a note on Tuesday. Similar shifts occurred in the late 1990s dot-com era and Covid rally, they added. "These dynamics provide further evidence that markets continue to move towards a more bubble-like state."
The bull case is that the midterms could alleviate some of the market's uncertainty and trigger a relief rally, Ciana noted. "Typically, risk assets such as the S&P 500 rebound after midterms unless more severe downside risks materialize."

articles.title_orig: Finland and Norway Hold ‘Frank’ Call With Putin on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Finland and Norway Hold ‘Frank’ Call With Putin on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Norway and Finland say they are not acting on behalf of other European leaders
The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.
Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re said the aim of the call had been to "convey messages directly regarding future negotiations" towards peace. An end to the conflict in Ukraine "will not be achieved through silence," Stubb said.
Neither side suggested the needle had been moved on ending the war, which began when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Although the Finnish leader said the conversation with Putin had been "frank and substantive," StÃ¸re added that there were "big differences in views" with Putin.
Several European leaders have recently shown willingness to engage with Russia directly, but both Stubb and StÃ¸re pointed out their initiative was taken in their capacity as neighbours of Russia, rather than on behalf of Europe as a whole.
"We've not set out to speak on behalf of anyone other than ourselves," StÃ¸re said.
Stubb added the call had been prepared in consultation with Ukraine and the US following a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the Nordic leaders and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo last week.
The first trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia talks since the start of the year are tentatively planned for early November in Abu Dhabi.
Zelensky later confirmed Stubb and StÃ¸re debriefed him after the call and said he was grateful for their "active support", while his Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the call had been "the right approach".
Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the 90-minute call - held from Helsinki - to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said.
StÃ¸re added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations."
The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered.
Putin also reaffirmed to the Nordic leaders what he views as the "root causes" of the conflict - his frequent shorthand for Ukraine's desire to exist as a sovereign state.
"A fair long-term peace settlement is possible only if Russia's legal interests are taken into account fully and unconditionally", Putin said.
All three parties reportedly agreed to continue their direct phone communication.
Rosenberg: Russia agrees to Ukraine talks but sees little to talk about in new peace push
There was no official EU reaction to the talks. The dialogue had not been coordinated with other European leaders, the Danish and Swedish prime ministers said. "I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo," commented Sweden's Ulf Kristersson.
Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Stubb had informed him that Europe's position on the upcoming talks in the United Arab Emirates was "moderately optimistic".
Relations between the US and Ukraine and its European allies have soured since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia, allowing Moscow to export oil to the America.
As the Trump administration's position on Russia has softened, several European leaders have said Europe should be trying to re-establish direct contacts with the Kremlin.
Stubb and StÃ¸re are the first European leaders to contact Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025.
Soon after, Putin visited Alaska for a summit with Trump, and from then on Europeans were further sidelined from Ukraine peace talks. Moscow regularly mocks European leaders and accuses the EU of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons.
But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good".
And although he said Moscow did not view Finland and Norway as speaking on behalf of Europe, on Tuesday Peskov conceded that Stubb and StÃ¸re's talks with Putin had been "very constructive and practical talks with the leaders of two key neighbouring states."

AT&T Inc. customers affected by two cybersecurity breaches in 2024 could start receiving payments soon, after a federal judge granted final approval to a $177 million class action settlement earlier this month.
AT&T ( T ) agreed to a settlement resolving a lawsuit alleging the company failed to implement adequate cybersecurity measures to protect customers' personal information following the 2024 data breaches.
On March 30, 2024, the company said that a data set released on the dark web contained AT&T customer information. On July 12, 2024, AT&T announced a second data breach in which limited data was illegally downloaded from an AT&T workspace on a third-party cloud platform.
The company denies any wrongdoing. The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas approved the deal on Oct. 2. If an appeal is not filed, the settlement's date is estimated to be on Nov. 12.
Read more: Just received a settlement? Here are 5 smart ways to use the money.
The deadline to submit a claim has passed, but customers were eligible to submit a claim and receive a payment if their personal information was compromised in one or both of the data breach incidents.
The deadline to submit a claim was Dec. 18, 2025, but customers who did submit a claim on time can visit TelecomDataSettlement.com for the most recent information.
Read more: Best high-yield savings account rates
Members who fall into the first settlement class and have a documented loss that occurred in 2019 or later are eligible for a cash payment of up to $5,000.
Those who fall into the second settlement class for losses that occurred on or after April 14, 2024, may receive a payment of up to $2,500.
As an alternative to a documented loss cash payment, eligible class members also had the option to submit a claim for a pro rata share of the remaining settlement fund after payment of settlement administration costs, attorneys' fees, costs, and service awards.
Payments must be distributed electronically or by paper check within 60 days of the effective date, or the official date when the terms of the settlement can no longer be appealed.

articles.title_orig: Flávio Bolsonaro's passports cancelled after he fails to surrender them
articles.title_zh: Flávio Bolsonaro's passports cancelled after he fails to surrender them
articles.content_orig:
Police in Brazil say they have cancelled the passports of the defeated right-wing presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, after he failed to comply with an order to surrender the documents.
On Monday, the Supreme Court ordered Bolsonaro to hand his passports over to police within 24 hours as part of an investigation into alleged money laundering, which he denies.
At the time, Bolsonaro said he had no plans to leave the country, and insisted that he would stay in Brazil to lead the opposition to his left-wing rival, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
However, the deadline has passed without the senator surrendering the passports, prompting speculation he may have left the country.
Federal officers are checking border crossings to establish if Bolsonaro may have travelled to neighbouring Argentina, according to a police source consulted by BBC News Brasil.
However, Argentine authorities have told the BBC there is no record of Bolsonaro entering their country through any border crossing.
Bolsonaro was already under investigation for alleged corruption over the financing of a film about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted of plotting a coup and is under house arrest.
In addition to that investigation, Brazil's Supreme Court ordered police on Tuesday to probe Flávio Bolsonaro's electoral campaign over alleged foreign funding.
The 45-year-old senator suffered a stinging defeat on Sunday when he was beaten by Lula in a presidential run-off, which Bolsonaro had been widely expected to win.
Opinion polls had put him narrowly ahead of Lula and analysts pointed out that Bolsonaro's win in the first round of the election on 4 October, meant he was likely to take victory in the run-off.
But after an early lead in the count, he was overtaken by the veteran incumbent, who became the first presidential candidate to overturn a first round loss to win in the second round.
Lula won 51.79% of the vote, compared to Bolsonaro's 48.21%.
Despite trailing by 4.4 million votes, Bolsonaro has not conceded and has called for the election to be annulled.
He argues that he was put at a disadvantage because polling was extended by two hours on election day - even though the extension was requested by both his party and that of his rival.
He called the extension, which was ordered by a Supreme Court justice, a "dirty trick".
However the party he represented, the Liberal Party, has accepted the result, although it did say that the extension of voting "merits investigation".

articles.title_orig: United ‘hijack’ text scare forces plane to turn back
articles.title_zh: United ‘hijack’ text scare forces plane to turn back
articles.content_orig:
LAS VEGAS (KSNV)  — The man accused of a terror threat on board a flight that took off from Las Vegas plans to enter a not guilty plea, his lawyer said Tuesday.
Attorney James Gallo appeared remotely in Las Vegas Justice Court on behalf of 25-year-old Dante Milne, who was arrested over the weekend. Milne himself did not appear in court.
Gallo informed Judge Rebecca Saxe that they would plead not guilty, and he requested a preliminary hearing. The next appearance is scheduled for Jan. 5, 2027.
Gallo declined to comment further when contacted by News 3 after the hearing.
Las Vegas Metropolitan Police said they took Milne into custody on Saturday at Harry Reid International Airport for alleged "terroristic threats" on a flight . bound for Newark Liberty Airportin New Jersey.
In air traffic control audio, someone can be heard saying that a flight attendant noticed a passenger writing in a text message that they wanted to hijack a plane.
According to an arrest report, a flight attendant told LVMPD that she saw a passenger receive a message from another passenger beginning with the words, "I'm gonna hijack."
"The message communicated a first-person declaration of intended violence involving hijacking the aircraft and crashing the recipient's row," the report alleged. "Both individuals were passengers aboard the aircraft referenced in the communication."
The attendant determined Milne was the sender based on the seating assignment and notified the lead flight attendant.
They then notified the captain once they passed 10,000 feet, and the crew decided to return to Las Vegas without a confrontation.
According to the report, officers detained Milne without incident after landing. He told officers he was in Las Vegas for a training program and had "beer and shots" before boarding the plane. He said the message was "banter between coworkers" and he did not plan to hijack the plane or harm anyone.
"Milne acknowledged the seriousness of the aircraft returning to Las Vegas and expressed remorse," LVMPD wrote.
The remaining passengers departed for Newark on Sunday.
Court records indicate Milne posted bond after his bail was set at $10,000.

articles.title_orig: Who Is Zhang Yiming? China's Richest Person Again
articles.title_zh: Who Is Zhang Yiming? China's Richest Person Again
articles.content_orig:
Beijing — ByteDance founder Zhang Yiming reclaimed the top spot on a list of China's richest people, driven by his company's push into artificial intelligence.
The rankings released by The Hurun Research Institute on Tuesday reflected that the country's high-tech sectors were rising while others, like the consumer sector and real estate, were under pressure.
The institute, which has published the list annually since 1999, found a record 1,529 people with more than 5 billion yuan (about $750 million), up 6.6% from last year.
The number of billionaires based on their net worth in U.S. dollars rose to 1,176, up 155 people - 176 more than in the U.S. That was slightly below the 1,185 people in 2021.
Zhang topped the list with $100 billion, up 43%, "almost all of it on the back of AI," and the amount was a record high for China's richest person, Rupert Hoogewerf, Hurun Report chairman, said in a statement. Hoogewerf noted that ByteDance's Doubao is China's most used AI assistant.
AI is the biggest single wealth engine on the list: 160 people - one in 10 - now make their money from AI, he said.
ByteDance is the parent company of popular short-video platforms TikTok and Douyin.
TikTok's U.S.-based operations were shifted to a new joint venture in January made up mostly of American investors due to years of national security-related concerns that almost got TikTok banned in the U.S. ByteDance still holds a minority stake in TikTok's U.S. arm.
One of the investors in TikTok's U.S. venture is Oracle, a tech company chaired by Larry Ellison. His son David Ellison is co-CEO of Skydance Corp., the parent company of CBS News.
Bottled water magnate Zhong Shanshan fell to second place on the list with $61 billion, down 23%, while Robin Zeng, chairman of CATL, the world's largest maker of batteries for electric vehicles, came in third, Hurun said.
Hurun cross-checked its information with entrepreneurs, regulators, industry experts and others to compile the list, while acknowledging limitations.
Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng, a new face on the list, ranked seventh. AI chipmaker Cambricon chair Chen Tianshi was 10th.
"This year's gains were polarised - entrepreneurs in AI, semiconductors and robotics surged ahead, whilst those in consumer, real estate and traditional manufacturing saw their wealth shrink - a two-speed economy," Hoogewerf said.
China last week said its economy grew 4.5% in the July-September quarter from a year ago, fueled by robust exports, moving closer to meeting its official annual growth target for 2026. For the entire year, Chinese leaders have set a growth target of 4.5% to 5%, down from last year's 5% expansion.
While some industries were thriving thanks to government support for technologies such as AI and electric vehicles, owners of small businesses reported tough times as their customers cut back on spending.
China's domestic demand has been weighed down by a yearslong downturn in its property market.
The Hurun list reflected that, as well.
Hoogewerf said Lei Jun, chairman of Chinese smart consumer electronics maker Xiaomi, was this year's "biggest faller," with his wealth halved to $25.1 billion. Consumer fortunes also fell across the board, Hoogewerf said.
"Today, for the first time ever, not a single mainland property developer remains in the Top 100 - the only property names left at the top are the Hong Kong landlord families," he said.

articles.title_orig: Everything Apple Announced This Week So Far: New iPad And MacBooks
articles.title_zh: Everything Apple Announced This Week So Far: New iPad And MacBooks
articles.content_orig:
Ahead of its 'Pro and Tell' event, the company has already launched a few new devices.
Apple wasn't done with its product reveals for the fall after unveiling the iPhone Duo , iPhone 18 Pro models and an array of smart home devices . Nor could it wait until the third event of the season, dubbed "Pro and Tell," to show off more gear.
The company got a string of announcements underway on Monday with the reveal of the long-awaited OLED iPad mini. Tuesday brought us an M6-powered iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro. It's expected that Apple will unveil a touchscreen MacBook as well.
Elsewhere, Apple released the latest versions of its operating systems. Among other things, those added more Siri AI features and made the assistant available in more languages. The company updated Apple Creator Studio with more AI features and creative tools as well.
We'll update this story if and when Apple makes more announcements. In the meantime, here's everything Apple has announced so far this week.
It feels like we've been waiting for forever for Apple to put an OLED display in the iPad mini but that day has finally arrived. The new display has double the peak brightness of the one on the previous model at 1,200 nits, and it has a 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio. The base storage remains the same at 128GB, though if you opt for 256GB or 512GB of storage, you can snag a variant with a nano-texture glass display. That'll cost you extra, naturally.
The company managed to squeeze in a larger screen — an 8.5-inch display rather than the 8.3-inch one in the previous model — without increasing the size of the tablet. In fact, the new iPad mini is slightly narrower than the last one, at 5.22 inches vs. 5.3 inches. It's lighter as well, with the Wi-Fi model coming in at 0.56 pounds (compared with 0.65 pounds last time) and the 5G variant weighing 0.58 pounds (versus 0.66 pounds). The latter, by the way, now boasts Apple's C2 modem, which is said to deliver up to 50 percent faster data speeds than the previous iPad mini. There's also Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread connectivity thanks to the N1 chip.
The OLED iPad mini — the eighth generation of the device — runs on the A20 Pro, the same chipset as the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. Apple says the SoC is capable of running large language models locally, in case you're into that kind of thing. Otherwise, the tablet should be notably faster than earlier models. It supports Apple Intelligence and Siri AI as well, of course. The chipset also boasts a 7-core GPU — two more cores than the A17 Pro, which powered the last-gen iPad mini.
On the camera front, there's a 12MP Center Stage lens on front of the tablet, which Apple has finally shifted to the landscape edge on the iPad mini. However, there's still no Face ID. The 12MP camera on the rear supports 4K 60fps video capture and Smart HDR 4.
The 8th-gen iPad mini has a sealed enclosure to help protect it from the elements. The tablet has an IP67 rating, meaning that it should withstand dust and being immersed in a meter of freshwater for up to 30 minutes, though I would advise against intentionally submerging your iPad mini.
As for battery life, Apple says that should be roughly the same as last time. The company says the new iPad mini should run for up to 10 hours when you're watching video or surfing the web over Wi-Fi. That drops down to nine hours if you're browsing over a cellular connection. If you have at least a 35W power adaptor, you'll be able to recharge the battery to 50 percent of its capacity in 30 minutes, Apple says.
The most interesting thing to me about this iPad mini is that it has Apple's first Acoustic Display, which the company says helps it deliver "an even better audio experience." It claims the tablet offers more volume and "punchier bass" thanks to woofers that "are paired through the display." Apple added that "custom tweeters are now hidden between the glass and aluminum enclosure for clearer highs." I'm definitely curious to find out how all of that sounds in practice.
Inevitably, the latest iPad mini comes with a price hike. It starts at $699, which is $150 more than the previous model after Apple increased the price of that in June . Pre-orders open on October 28, and the tablet will hit shelves on November 6.
On Tuesday, Apple gave the iMac and MacBook Pro spec bumps. The desktop and laptop now each have the M6 chipset , which recently debuted in the Mac mini .
Let's start with the new iMac . Apple says the M6's dual 16-core neural engine enables it to deliver up to five times faster on-device AI performance (for Siri AI, Apple Intelligence and local LLMs) than the previous-gen iMac from 2024 , which had the M4 chipset. The M6 is said to deliver up to 1.5 times faster performance than the M4 for daily tasks, up to two times faster graphics performance (for photo editing etc.) and up to two times higher gaming performance with ray tracing.
The base-level M6 has 10 CPU cores (two super, three performance and two efficiency cores) and a 10-core CPU, compared with eight of each in the M4. There's the option to have a 12-core M6, in which case your desktop will have four Thunderbolt 4 ports instead of the two that the base model has. The four-port model has a nano-texture glass option as well.
Elsewhere, Apple has introduced its N1 networking chip to the iMac. As such, the computer has support for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread connectivity. It also has the option to add a 2.5Gb Ethernet port, an upgrade from gigabit Ethernet on the M4 iMac.
Specs otherwise are the same as last time. You'll still get a 24-inch 4.5K Super Retina display, a 12MP Center Stage camera, a six‑speaker Dolby Atmos system, at least 16GB of RAM and 256GB of base storage. The dimensions are identical too, though the M6 iMac is a touch lighter than the previous gen at 9.7 pounds (versus 9.74 pounds). Don't expect any changes to the color options either — the new iMac is still available in blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange and silver.
One other thing that's staying the same? The starting price, at least after the $200 increase that Apple gave the M4 iMac over the summer. The new model starts at $1,499, and the four-port version will run you at least $1,699. Pre-orders open October 28 and you'll be able to pick one up in store on November 6.
The latest 14-inch MacBook Pro has the 12-core version of the M6 chipset and the N1 networking chip for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support. Those appear to be the only spec changes this time.
Compared with the previous-gen 14-inch MBP, which had an M5 SoC, Apple says the M6 model offers up to 30 percent faster graphics performance and up to 25 percent faster AI workloads. It's said to deliver up to 1.3 faster rendering performance with ray tracing in Blender, up to 1.2 times faster image-processing performance in Affinity and up to 1.3 faster project build performance for compiling code in Xcode.
It doesn't seem like this will be a massive upgrade for folks with an M5 model. However, if you have an older MacBook Pro (or really need those incremental improvements from the previous gen), it might be worth making the switch.
Either way, creatives might want to take note of all the updates that are rolling out for Apple Creative Studio . Apple has given Final Cut Pro a long-awaited quality-of-life upgrade by letting you pull clips from the primary storyline and place them anywhere on the timeline, which seems like very basic functionality to have! MotionVFX is integrated into the app on Mac as well, so you'll have thousands of elements at your fingertips for your video edits.
If you have a Mac that supports Apple Intelligence and is set to US English, Logic Pro has an "intelligent assistant" powered by OpenAI that's available in beta. The app has an an enhanced Stem Splitter that can now separate drums as well. In addition, Keynote, Pages and Numbers now have a chatbot you can use to adjust presentations, documents and spreadsheets.

articles.title_orig: Boeing Stock Plunges After Earnings. 737 Progress Is Not Fast Enough.
articles.title_zh: Boeing Stock Plunges After Earnings. 737 Progress Is Not Fast Enough.
articles.content_orig:
Boeing doesn't expect to significantly ramp up output of its best-selling 737 Max aircraft until the second half of 2027 as it grapples with a slower-than-expected pace of wing production.
CEO Kelly Ortberg said Tuesday on the company's quarterly earnings call that Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. It has been manufacturing about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month.
Ortberg had told investors last month that the production stabilize was taking a "little bit longer" than expected becuase of the wings production pace.
Boeing stock was down about 9% during the call.
"I know everybody wants us to go faster but we're going to do it right," Ortberg told CNBC's Phil LeBeau in an interview Tuesday.
Ortberg reiterated the company's priority in stabilizing production on Tuesday.
"Looking ahead, expectations are rising, and they should," Ortberg said in a note to staff on Tuesday. "That means elevating our performance through lean, productivity and efficiency improvements in our day-to-day work while upholding our high levels of safety and quality."
Aircraft production and deliveries are key to Boeing's recovery since the bulk of an aircraft's price is paid when the customer receives it.
The company also reported Tuesday that it narrowed its losses in the third quarter, thanks to a boost from its defense unit.
For the three months ended Sept. 30, Boeing reported a net loss of $116 million, or 26 cents a share, compared with a $5.34 billion loss, or $7.14 per share, a year earlier. Adjusting for one-time items, the company posted a loss of 34 cents a share. A year earlier, Boeing had taken a nearly $5 billion charge on its long-delayed 777X aircraft program.
Revenue climbed 4% on the year to $24.19 billion. Free cash flow rose to $464 million from $238 million in the third quarter of 2025.
The company's defense unit revenue jumped 15% in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.94 billion.
Here's what Boeing reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street analysts expected, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:
Boeing delivered 161 commercial airplanes in the third quarter, one more jet than a year earlier.
Revenue in the all-important commercial aircraft business fell 3% to $10.72 billion. The unit had a negative operating margin of 6.5% because of a "less favorable delivery mix, higher projected costs associated with future production rate adjustments and higher estimated supply chain costs," Boeing said.
Ortberg told staff in a memo that the manufacturer has "more work to do."
The manufacturer had some wins lately. The U.S. Navy tapped Boeing to develop its next-generation fighter jet.
And the Federal Aviation Administration last week signed off on the 737 Max 10 , the largest in the Max family. That followed the approval of the 737 Max 7 in August and marked the final certifications for the aircraft line.

articles.title_orig: Pope says ‘there is no such thing as a holy war’ in message to religious leaders
articles.title_zh: Pope says ‘there is no such thing as a holy war’ in message to religious leaders
articles.content_orig:
Pope John Paul II attends an interreligious peace meeting in Assisi, Italy, in this Oct. 27, 1986, file photo. (CNS/L'Osservatore Romano)
Send your thoughts to Letters to the Editor . Learn more
This is not an easy time to work across lines of difference — especially across religious differences. Particularly since the attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, I have heard many Jewish and Muslim friends express hesitation and fear about working in interfaith spaces.
Amid these challenges, it is worth reflecting on the example of St. Pope John Paul II and his historic gathering in Assisi 40 years ago. He convened the World Day of Prayer for Peace — bringing leaders from a wide range of religions to pray alongside one another. He tried to strike a challenging balance — to gather international, interfaith leaders to each pray for peace while also being clear that his own Catholic Church has the truest religious understanding.
In the face of rising antisemitism and Islamophobia in the United States, this anniversary is an opportunity for Catholics to consider how we can be good neighbors.
The Assisi meeting had a lasting impact on John Paul II, which we can echo today.
As John Borelli, who served over 16 years at the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops in ecumenical and interreligious affairs, told me on a recent recording for my podcast, " Our Little Portion ," this first meeting developed the idea of a "Spirit of Assisi." In his 1986 annual Christmas Address to the Curia, John Paul II spoke as if he could not stop thinking about the Assisi gathering, and seemed to consider it one of the most important events of his papacy.
This "Spirit of Assisi" has been both celebrated and contested. One writer called the Assisi gathering a " disaster ," and claimed that the end result of Assisi was the sense that Catholics believe that their religion is just one among many — rather than the one true faith.
But many others believe that the Assisi gathering was a revolution in interfaith dialogue, understanding and work toward peace. The goal of the gathering was not syncretism or a blending together into one unified faith, the goal was to provide space for distinction. Catholics, of course, hold that ours is the one true faith. Peacefully coming together to pray for common goals and dialogue together does not water down our traditions. In many cases, it can strengthen our own understanding of our tradition.
In a reflection on the Vatican website , Cardinal Roger Etchegaray, one of the planners of the original gathering, wrote about how that the leaders were moved to tears during the closing ceremonies, including a particularly moving experience during the finale when, outside St. Francis' Basilica, "some young Jews leaped up on to the platform to offer olive branches to us, and to Muslims first of all, I found myself wiping the tears from my own face."
The Holy Spirit was moving, and the movement continues to this day. John Paul II gathered interfaith leaders in Assisi multiple times, and Pope Benedict XVI continued the tradition in his own way — including adding secular humanists to the group. Indeed, Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger was one of those leaders with concerns about the first Assisi gathering, but went on to make the tradition his own as pope.
Rabbi David Rosen attended multiple Assisi gatherings. In a recent interview with "Our Little Portion," he recalled John Paul II's powerful words to him at Assisi: "You know I have said, 'You are our dearly beloved elder brother of the original covenant, never broken and never to be broken.' " Assisi was, in many ways, the next step following the Nostra Aetate document of the Second Vatican Council that decried antisemitism in all of its forms and rebutted the idea of placing the blame for Jesus' death at the collective feet of the Jewish people.
Rosen said that interfaith engagement on areas of shared values is necessary — to not do so would be to betray those very values.
Similarly, Homayra Ziad , a scholar who was featured in the film "The Sultan and the Saint," said that shared understanding of humanity made in the image of God calls us to greater understanding. She told me:
If I believe we are each created in the image of the divine, then I am called to ardently seek that divinity in myself and in every single created being, to establish a deeper and more sustained connection with the higher energy that binds us all — or as Pope John Paul II said, "the deepest and most vivifying sources where …[humanity's] conscience is formed and upon which is founded the moral action of all people."
Through times of discord, interfaith leaders have returned to Assisi — during the Cold War, during the Balkans war, and following the September 11 attacks. They show us that even amid war, chaos and polarization, dialogue and shared action are still possible.
What, then, does the Spirit of Assisi mean for us?
Rosen defined it this way:
A recognition that we have an obligation not only to know one another but to work together especially for peace. … And for its prayer to be its own prayer. Neither syncretistic nor having to water it down in order to accommodate others, and then at the same time coming together, affirming a unity of human brotherhood.
If we are to be faithful to the Spirit of Assisi in this generation, it is going to require that we, too, find our own way of living out the truth of the Catholic faith in a way that deepens our understanding as we walk with people of other faiths. This means standing with our Muslim and Jewish brothers and sisters as they face increased hate and attacks on their religious freedom — while understanding that our own religious freedom is intertwined with theirs. Ultimately, it requires that we find inspiration to love as Jesus loved — including all of our neighbors and even our enemies.
Here, St. Francis provides us with a powerful example. In the middle of the Fifth Crusade, Francis chose to cross enemy lines to meet with Sultan Malik al-Kamil. Little is known about this meeting, other than a few essential facts: Francis preached to the sultan and engaged in dialogue with him, and he returned home alive, against all odds.
Franciscan Br. William Short has written that the meeting was unimaginable, given the hostilities of the time and the dehumanizing ways Muslims and Catholics viewed each other.
Ziad pointed out that Francis and Sultan al-Kamil were uniquely prepared for their encounter. She noted that the sultan "grew up educated both religiously and in secular matters, surrounded by scholars, scientists, and artists; knowledge and the sharing of knowledge was seen as a value and he liked to surround himself with people of learning." She also pointed out that the Quran and early Muslim tradition have high regard for Christian holy people.
She told me, "In many ways, both [the sultan] and St Francis had been 'prepared,' in different ways, for an encounter where they could be changed by the other, indeed even their forms of devotion could be shaped by the other."
Still, it was not easy for Francis or the sultan to cross "enemy lines." Gathering interfaith leaders in Assisi was not easy for John Paul II, Benedict XVI or Pope Francis. Pope Leo XIV's calls for world peace are not easy, either. But amid war, hate and division, each of us must do our part to build bridges of understanding and work together for the common good.
Ziad posed the question that our Catholic institutions need to answer:
"How can religious institutions invest in preparing our young people to engage difference with true sincerity, curiosity and divine love, understanding that the traditions we misunderstand as closed loops were shaped every step of the way through interreligious encounters?"
Indeed, as we commemorate this 40th anniversary of St. Pope John Paul II's first gathering in Assisi, we must continue the work of a more peaceful way forward for all religions.

articles.title_orig: Iran talks Middle East security, urges region to get US influence out
articles.title_zh: Iran talks Middle East security, urges region to get US influence out
articles.content_orig:
The State Department has ordered non-emergency government personnel and their families to evacuate Saudi Arabia following a surge in missile and drone strikes targeting civilian airports and critical infrastructure across the kingdom.
In a security alert issued Tuesday, the U.S. warned that ongoing hostilities by Iran-backed Houthi forces have caused severe travel disruptions and civilian casualties, prompting strict travel restrictions for American personnel and warnings of wider regional spillover.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," according to the alert.
"The hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area."
Flight operations remain severely disrupted across major transit hubs, including Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport , where only limited routes are running, alongside significant delays at facilities in Jeddah and Dammam.
U.S. officials urged private citizens to exercise extreme caution, consider overland transit alternatives via operational borders like the King Fahd Causeway, and strictly abide by local regulations barring the filming or sharing of attack sites and counter-missile activity.
Ali Khamenei / Iranian Leader Press Office / Anadolu via Getty Images
President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday praised the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei as a founding pillar of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF), telling delegates in Moscow that Russia remembers Iran’s former supreme leader "with gratitude."
"You have quite rightly mentioned the role of the late Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was indeed one of the most active participants in the establishment of our forum, and we rightly remember this with gratitude," Putin said, according to Iranian state-run Press TV .
Iran was central to the forum’s origins, with the initiative first proposed in Tehran in 2001 and the organization formally established in 2008.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met on Tuesday on the sidelines of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit in Moscow to strengthen bilateral energy and economic ties.
“They discussed expanding political, economic, trade and energy cooperation, including joint projects in the oil and gas sectors,” the Iranian government said in a post on X .
Discussing natural gas exports, Pezeshkian highlighted Iran’s position as the world's third-largest producer, behind the United States and Russia and called for deeper strategic coordination.
"Pezeshkian emphasized that global developments necessitate joint technical-engineering cooperation and strategic governance across international energy markets," the Iranian government said in a later readout.
Vice President JD Vance defended President Donald Trump's bold midterm election year pressure on Iran's threats in the Strait of Hormuz, acknowledging its causing higher gas prices globally, but warning the U.S. cannot be held hostage every time a Middle East leader "throws a tantrum."
"I want to speak to the voters who are undecided: You'll hear many say that gas prices are too high," Vance told his rally in Howell, Michigan , on Tuesday. "Ladies and gentlemen, I understand that it's true, but the deeper truth is that the price of gas goes up each time a foreign leader in the Middle East throws a tantrum.
"That's been true, by the way, since before I was alive, starting in the 1970s.
"But what's different? What's different about this country's and this leaderships' agenda ?
"And what's different about the Democrats is that the Democrats talk about high gas prices, even though their policies have made us more vulnerable to the foreign despots in the first place."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio is traveling Tuesday aboard Air Force One with President Donald Trump in his concurrent capacity as national security adviser, securing direct access to the commander-in-chief, an administration official confirmed to Fox News.
With Trump maintaining an active domestic travel schedule ahead of the midterms, the transit time provides a dedicated window for high-level national security consultations.
"He needs time with the president on all kinds of issues," according to a White House official.
"The president will be on the go, so being on the plane with him gives him a chance to talk to him about these items."
The in-flight briefings come at a critical juncture for U.S. Middle East strategy.
Over the last 24 hours alone, the White House has confronted an escalating maritime blockade in the Strait of Hormuz marked by active Iranian mine detonations, Houthi strikes targeting Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura refinery, and the emergency evacuation of non-essential U.S. personnel from the kingdom.
Fox News' Gillian Turner contributed to this report.
President Donald Trump highlighted incoming shipments of Venezuelan crude Tuesday as a direct economic cushion against rising fuel prices spurred by the 9-month-old conflict with Iran, pointing to alternative energy imports during a campaign departure for Texas.
Speaking to reporters ahead of rallies alongside Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, Trump praised recent surges in consumer confidence before confirming plans to showcase an arriving oil tanker carrying Venezuelan crude destined for processing at Gulf Coast facilities.
"We took over Venezuela very successfully, and they've sent me as a gift, a boatload of a million barrels of oil, and I'm giving that to the United States of America," Trump told reporters on the tarmac from Joint Base Andrews, framing the imports as a tangible benefit of his administration's pressure campaign.
"We're going to accept a million barrels of oil , and I'm going to give it to you people to use it the way you want. And we're going to have oil prices are going to be dropping very sharply."
The administration has increasingly relied on Western Hemisphere energy flows to offset global supply contractions caused by maritime blockades in the Strait of Hormuz and repeated strikes by Iran-aligned proxies on regional Gulf infrastructure.
With domestic pump prices edging above previous-term averages just a week before the November midterms, the White House has maintained that foreign oil seizures, increased Caribbean imports, and record domestic production will neutralize temporary spikes until the Middle East war is resolved.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is warning about voter turnout in the elections underway Tuesday.
"We're at war for our home 🚨," Netanyahu added in a second post. "Muslim Brotherhood supporters are raiding the polling stations and stealing the elections.
"Go out and vote, recover it!!"
Cars flying Netanyahu's Likud party flags drove through Jerusalem blaring the Islamic call to prayer and urging supporters to cast their ballots because "Arabs are voting," witnesses said.
"If we don't wake up now, we'll find ourselves with a government of Mansour Abbas and Ahmed Tibi," Netanyahu wrote in a post, referring to two leading Palestinian Arab politicians in Israel.
Turnout reached 55.7% in the first nine hours of voting, the elections committee said, the fastest pace on record.
Arabs, mostly of Palestinian heritage, make up about 21% of Israel's population of 10 million and have traditionally voted at lower rates than Jewish Israelis.
Tibi, a candidate from an Arab party, said strong turnout among Israel's Arab minority would "pave the way for an alternative government and change the grave reality."
Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of the Arab Balad party, wrote on X that long lines outside polling stations should bring "pride and joy to anyone who believed in democracy."

articles.title_orig: Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after presidential election loss, reports say
articles.title_zh: Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after presidential election loss, reports say
articles.content_orig:
Far-right senator on plane to US after missing deadline to hand over his passport since loss to Lula
The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro has reportedly fled Brazil and is on his way to the United States after losing Sunday’s presidential election to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
A report by the news website Metrópoles , citing people close to the politician’s family, said he was en route to the US. “The plane is in flight,” Metrópoles reported, without making clear where it had departed from.
Bolsonaro allies told Metrópoles that he would land in Florida on Tuesday afternoon and planned to request political asylum. “The Donald Trump administration has been informed,” the website added.
Allies also confirmed to the Folha de S Paulo newspaper that he was on his way to the US, and said the escape plan had been “organized and enabled by a lawyer close to the Bolsonaro clan”.
“They say the flight should land in a few hours,” the newspaper added.
The news network CNN Brasil reported that Bolsonaro had fled to the US with his wife and two daughters in the early hours of this morning.
Lawmakers from Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s arrest and requested that his name be put on Interpol’s Red Notice list.
Bolsonaro had not been seen since Monday and missed a Tuesday-morning deadline to hand his passport to the federal police, fuelling rumours that he may have fled Brazil after losing on Sunday.
A report in the Brazilian newspaper O Globo said that during a meeting with friends and lawyers on Monday, the defeated candidate had appeared “possessed and made it clear he was afraid of being arrested”.
A supreme court justice cancelled Bolsonaro’s passport minutes after the result in a ruling related to a criminal case against the senator. He had until 11am to surrender the document to the federal police, but did not appear.
Bolsonaro has had Italian citizenship since 2023 and reportedly possesses a passport from the European country.
The Argentinian news website Infobae reported that on Monday night he reportedly fled to Argentina, where he was expected to board a private jet in Puerto Iguazú bound for the US, but the plane did not take off.
Bolsonaro, who has yet to concede defeat to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, posted a video on Monday in which, commenting on the cancellation of his passport, he said: “I never thought about leaving the country.”
One of the senator’s brothers, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, who is in self-imposed exile in the US, had said in an interview last Friday that his brother should leave Brazil if he lost.
The Brazilian newspaper Folha de S Paulo reported that allies in the Bolsonaro family’s inner circle had been told that he had indeed left for Argentina and intended to travel from there to the US.
As there is no record of him passing through any regular Brazilian immigration checkpoint, the federal police are trying to establish from Argentinian authorities whether there is any record of him entering the country.
The Argentinian channel Todo Noticias reported that the senator had reportedly crossed the border into Argentina on foot and abandoned plans to board the plane once news of his movements leaked.
Bolsonaro was told to surrender his passport over a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating him for possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme worth about £680m ($905m) involving betting companies.
The senator’s possible flight makes the future of the far right after the presidential election even more uncertain. The family patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro, is under house arrest for attempting a coup, and one of his sons is in the US and the whereabouts of another unclear.
after newsletter promotion
Eduardo Bolsonaro has an outstanding arrest warrant against him in Brazil, after being sentenced to four years in prison for trying to interfere in his father’s trial by lobbying Donald Trump to impose sanctions on the justices hearing the case.
Political scientist Magna Inácio, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais, believes a power vacuum may now emerge within the right.
“The resistance of Brazilian voters to handing victory to this more extremist camp sends a signal that the right leadership is now up for grabs,” she said.
Since Jair Bolsonaro, then a career congressman with few laws to his name, surprisingly won the presidency in 2018, there has effectively been no right wing in Brazil, only the far-right Bolsonarismo movement.
Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right, believes the fact that three Bolsonaros are now potentially out of the picture could trigger a “shift in power” away from blood ties.
“I think there is a tendency for power to move away from the sons,” said Rocha, noting that before the election, polls showed Jair Bolsonaro supporters preferred other potential candidates over his eldest son, including Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who was recently elected senator, and the São Paulo governor, Tarcísio de Freitas.
Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly did not want to run because he thought a presidential campaign would turn his life into “hell”, and believed his re-election to the senate was assured. But with Eduardo, his father’s “plan A”, now living in the US, the senator was chosen to run.
Most observers agree that Flávio lacks his father’s charisma. He had a 24-year political career in which he passed very few laws as a state legislator and senator, and the only previous time he ran for executive office was for mayor of Rio de Janeiro in 2016, when he fainted during a televised debate and finished fourth.
Even in a family frequently embroiled in legal trouble he stood out, facing longstanding criminal allegations, including suspicions that he embezzled part of his staff’s salaries, as well as more recent accusations.
Even so, 48.21% of Brazilians voted for Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday, which many analysts see as both an anti-Lula vote and a vote for whomever Jair Bolsonaro had chosen.
Inácio believes the struggle over the Bolsonaro legacy will also play out among family members who remain in Brazil, including Michelle and Bolsonaro’s other political sons, the senator-elect Carlos Bolsonaro and congressman-elect Jair Renan Bolsonaro, who publicly do not get along with their stepmother.
“Michelle clearly has a political project of her own, but she is likely to face strong resistance from the two stepsons who are in congress. It is only a matter of time before tensions between them grow,” said the political scientist.
